extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing whether patent claims recite eligible subject matter under the USPTO’s 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance (IEG), including application of Step 1, Step 2A, and Step 2B analyses and life-science–specific considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category of invention (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a machine, composition, process, or manufacture (e.g., an internal combustion engine, a vaccine, a method for loading BIOS), Step 1 is YES and the claim is within a statutory category. Examples: an internal combustion engine (machine/combination of mechanical parts), vaccines (composition of matter), methods for loading BIOS (process).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify any judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the claim elements to see if they recite an exception (e.g., mathematical relationship, product of nature). If an exception is recited, proceed to determine whether the claim is directed to that exception (Steps 2A/2B) or whether other limitations remove it from being 'directed to' the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) for eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret the claim under its broadest reasonable interpretation when performing the eligibility analysis and when identifying closest natural counterparts for nature-based claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the BRI to identify embodiments encompassed by the claim (e.g., a vaccine claim's BRI may include a peptide mixed with water). The BRI affects whether a claim reads on a natural counterpart or a mere combination of natural products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics (nature-based products)
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims reciting nature-based products, compare the claimed product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart to determine if it has markedly different characteristics (structural or functional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed nature-based product exhibits marked differences from the natural counterpart (e.g., a nucleotide mutation in a live attenuated virus; formalin-induced chemical modification of a virus), it is not a 'product of nature' exception. Structural differences that produce functional changes support eligibility (Myriad and Chakrabarty analogies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixtures and carriers: assess whether combination changes properties
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim recites a mixture of naturally occurring components, determine whether mixing changes the structure, function, or other properties of the components in a marked way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere mixture (e.g., peptide + water) that does not alter the components' structure/function and is routine/conventional does not show markedly different characteristics and thus may be an ineligible 'product of nature' (compare Funk Brothers). Conversely, reciting a specific carrier form (e.g., cream/emulsion) that imposes structural/physical changes can confer eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A analysis (when applicable)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether the claim as a whole is nonetheless not directed to the exception because it integrates the exception into a practical application or recites markedly different characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that integrate a mathematical relationship into a technical control scheme (e.g., Arrhenius equation used to control press timing) or that recite nature-based products with markedly different characteristics can be resolved at Step 2A (NO to exception) without proceeding to full Step 2B analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: 'significantly more' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is determined to be directed to a judicial exception at Step 2A, analyze whether additional elements, or an ordered combination of elements, provide significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for meaningful limitations that limit the use of the exception and improve a technical field (e.g., ordered combination of sensors, specific control systems that improve rubber molding or engine technology). Generic or routine computer components used only to implement an abstract idea typically do not supply 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether mathematical relationships are integrated into a technical improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims reciting mathematical relationships or calculations, evaluate whether the claim merely tells practitioners to use the formula in isolation or whether it integrates the mathematical concept into a technical process or device to improve technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely instruct calculation/comparison are suspect; claims that use the mathematical relationship as part of a control system or specific apparatus that improves a technological process (e.g., initiating a signal to open a press when reaction time equivalence is reached) amount to 'significantly more' and are eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered combination and meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether additional claim limitations, when viewed in combination and as an ordered arrangement, provide meaningful limits on the use of any judicial exception and contribute to a technical improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if individual elements are conventional or components of an exception, their particular ordered combination may demonstrate improved functioning in a technical field and thus render a claim eligible (examples: specific arrangements of sensors, processors, valves in engine/EGR control).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use streamlined analysis and when to document reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: If eligibility is self-evident (e.g., claim plainly amounts to significantly more or does not recite an exception), examiners may use a streamlined analysis without issuing a written rejection; however, remarks may be added to an Office action or reasons for allowance to clarify the basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where streamlined analysis applies include claims that clearly recite a statutory category and meaningful technical limitations (internal combustion engine example, BIOS loading method). If record would benefit from clarification, add remarks that identify any recited exceptions and explain why the claim nonetheless provides meaningful limitations or improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice-note: how to frame a rejection or allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: If rejecting for lack of eligibility, an examiner should identify the specific exceptions in the claim and explain why the claimed subject matter lacks markedly different characteristics or why additional claim elements/combination do not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper rejection should point to the nature-based products or abstract ideas in the claim, explain comparison to natural counterparts, and state why combining components is routine, conventional, or fails to change properties in a marked way. Conversely, reasons for allowance may note that claimed limitations provide meaningful limitations and improve the technical field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional vs. structural change consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether claimed changes are functional, structural, or both; structural changes that produce functional differences are persuasive for eligibility, and sometimes functional changes inseparable from structural changes will suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live attenuated virus example: nucleotide mutation (structural) resulted in reduced virulence (functional), supporting markedly different characteristics. In other cases functional changes alone may be sufficient if they are inseparable from an underlying structural change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular/unconventional device analysis (Step 2B for nature-based claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims that are directed to nature-based products or exceptions, assess whether the claim recites a particular and unconventional device or implementation that amounts to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a vaccine delivery device comprising a coated microneedle array (an unconventional delivery device relative to syringes) may be eligible under Step 2B because the recited particular device can provide significantly more than the nature-based exception alone.
